title: "Downscaling CMIP6 projections of weather extremes over Chile: a CNN super-resolution approach"

abstract: |
  Chile spans very different climates, from the arid Atacama to sub-polar
  Patagonia, in a strip rarely wider than 200 km between the Pacific and the
  Andes. CMIP6 models lack the spatial resolution needed to resolve steep
  elevation gradients and terrain heterogeneity, limiting their ability to
  accurately estimate changes in extreme heat and rainfall from direct model
  output alone. We use a convolutional neural network (CNN) and quantile
  mapping to bias-correct and downscale 2071–2100 SSP5-8.5 projections of
  extreme weather indices (Rx1day, Rx5day, TXx, R10mm) from their native
  1° resolution to 0.05°, using CR2MET as the reference dataset. In held-out
  years, the CNN decreases Rx1day error by 47% against bilinear interpolation.

  The downscaled projections from 20+ CMIP6 models agree on warming in every
  subregion, and most project a drier Central Chile and Northern Patagonia on
  average. The Rx1day change depends strongly on latitude: Central Chile
  (30–38°S) tends toward less extreme rainfall under SSP5-8.5, while the
  wettest day of the year becomes wetter in Northern Chile and Patagonia. TXx
  rises in every subregion, from 3.6 °C in Southern Patagonia to 4.9 °C in the
  north. Over Central Chile frequency decreases more than intensity: R10mm
  declines 29% against 11% for Rx5day and 6% for Rx1day, and GEV fits estimate
  the 2-year event 8% lower with the 100-year event unchanged — the coast loses
  ordinary winter rain but not its largest floods. Testing whether extreme
  precipitation changes follow expected subtropical drying (circulation
  control) or intensify with atmospheric moisture (thermodynamic control), only
  7 of 241 land cells approximately follow Clausius–Clapeyron scaling, with the
  largest deviations over the drying latitudes — pointing to circulation rather
  than thermodynamic control.

summary: "A CNN super-resolution approach to downscaling CMIP6 extreme-weather indices over Chile from 1° to 0.05°, cutting Rx1day error by 47% against bilinear interpolation."
